subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 45-year-old woman has an anterior mediastinal mass on chest CT. Her physician reviews the four classic 'T' tumors of the anterior mediastinum when constructing the differential diagnosis.
question: Which of the following is one of the classic '4 Ts' of anterior mediastinal masses?

options.text: Neurofibroma
Thymic neoplasm
Esophageal cancer
Multiple myeloma
Bronchogenic cyst

explanation_correct: The normal mediastinum contains the heart, thymus, lymph nodes, esophagus, and aorta. The classic anterior mediastinal masses are the 4 Ts: thyroid (substernal goiter), thymic neoplasm, teratoma, and terrible lymphoma. A thymic neoplasm is therefore one of these classic lesions.

explanation_incorrect.A: Neurofibroma is a neurogenic tumor associated with the posterior mediastinum, not the anterior compartment.
explanation_incorrect.C: Esophageal cancer arises in the posterior mediastinum and may spread to the middle mediastinum, not the anterior compartment.
explanation_incorrect.D: Multiple myeloma is associated with the posterior mediastinum, not the anterior compartment.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bronchogenic cysts are found in the middle mediastinum, not the anterior compartment.

educationalObjective: The anterior mediastinal '4 Ts' are thyroid (substernal goiter), thymic neoplasm, teratoma, and lymphoma.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A chest CT shows a fluid-filled cyst in the middle mediastinum adjacent to the central airways. The radiologist lists the lesions most typically found in the middle mediastinal compartment.
question: Which lesion is most typically associated with the middle mediastinum?

options.text: Substernal goiter
Teratoma
Lymphoma
Bronchogenic cyst
Neurofibroma

explanation_correct: Common middle mediastinal lesions include metastases, hiatal hernia, and bronchogenic cysts. A bronchogenic cyst adjacent to the central airways fits this compartment. Although some pathologies such as lymphoma, lung cancer, and abscess can occur in any compartment, these are the classic middle mediastinal associations.

explanation_incorrect.A: Substernal goiter (thyroid) is a classic anterior mediastinal mass, not a middle mediastinal lesion.
explanation_incorrect.B: Teratoma is one of the 4 Ts of the anterior mediastinum.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lymphoma (terrible lymphoma) is classically an anterior mediastinal mass, though nodal tumors can occur in any compartment.
explanation_incorrect.E: Neurofibroma is a neurogenic tumor of the posterior mediastinum.

educationalObjective: Middle mediastinal lesions classically include metastases, hiatal hernia, and bronchogenic cysts.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 62-year-old man has a well-circumscribed posterior mediastinal mass on imaging. The differential includes tumors classically found in the posterior compartment.
question: Which tumor is classically associated with the posterior mediastinum?

options.text: Neurogenic tumor such as neurofibroma
Thymoma
Substernal goiter
Hiatal hernia
Teratoma

explanation_correct: Posterior mediastinal masses classically include esophageal cancer, neurogenic tumors such as neurofibroma, and multiple myeloma. A neurogenic tumor is therefore a classic posterior mediastinal lesion.

explanation_incorrect.B: Thymic neoplasm (thymoma) is an anterior mediastinal tumor.
explanation_incorrect.C: Substernal goiter is a thyroid mass of the anterior mediastinum.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hiatal hernia is associated with the middle mediastinum, not the posterior mediastinum.
explanation_incorrect.E: Teratoma is an anterior mediastinal germ cell tumor.

educationalObjective: Posterior mediastinal masses classically include esophageal cancer, neurogenic tumors (eg, neurofibroma), and multiple myeloma.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 66-year-old man develops fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, and chest pain 8 days after coronary artery bypass grafting. He has purulent drainage from his sternal wound.
question: Which diagnosis and time course best fit this presentation?

options.text: Fibrosing mediastinitis due to Histoplasma, presenting months to years later
Pneumomediastinum due to a ruptured pulmonary bleb
Acute mediastinitis as a postoperative complication of cardiothoracic surgery within 14 days
Esophageal cancer with posterior mediastinal invasion
Anterior mediastinal teratoma with malignant transformation

explanation_correct: Mediastinitis is inflammation of mediastinal tissues and is commonly due to postoperative complications of cardiothoracic procedures within 14 days. Clinical features include fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, chest pain, and sternal wound drainage, matching this patient's presentation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Chronic fibrosing mediastinitis due to Histoplasma is a late, insidious process, not an acute postoperative infection with sternal wound drainage within days.
explanation_incorrect.B: Pneumomediastinum presents with chest pain, crepitus, and subcutaneous emphysema, not fever, leukocytosis, and purulent sternal drainage.
explanation_incorrect.D: Esophageal cancer is a posterior mediastinal malignancy that does not present as an acute postoperative sternal wound infection.
explanation_incorrect.E: Teratoma is an anterior mediastinal germ cell tumor, not a cause of postoperative fever and sternal drainage.

educationalObjective: Postoperative mediastinitis follows cardiothoracic surgery within 14 days and causes fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, chest pain, and sternal wound drainage.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 42-year-old woman from the Ohio River Valley presents with progressive dyspnea and facial swelling. Imaging shows a dense fibrotic mass in the mediastinum encasing the superior vena cava and pulmonary veins. There is no fever or leukocytosis.
question: Which underlying process and organism most likely explain this presentation?

options.text: Acute postoperative mediastinitis within 14 days of cardiothoracic surgery
Boerhaave syndrome with esophageal perforation after repetitive vomiting
Metastatic carcinoma involving middle mediastinal lymph nodes
Anterior mediastinal lymphoma with superior vena cava compression
Chronic fibrosing mediastinitis with connective tissue proliferation, commonly due to Histoplasma capsulatum

explanation_correct: Chronic mediastinitis, also called fibrosing mediastinitis, results from increased proliferation of connective tissue in the mediastinum. Histoplasma capsulatum is a common cause, and the resulting dense fibrosis can encase mediastinal vessels and cause obstructive symptoms without acute infection signs.

explanation_incorrect.A: Postoperative mediastinitis occurs within 14 days of cardiothoracic surgery with fever and sternal drainage, not as a chronic fibrotic process.
explanation_incorrect.B: Boerhaave syndrome is an acute esophageal perforation following violent vomiting that causes mediastinitis and pneumomediastinum, not insidious fibrosing mediastinitis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Metastatic carcinoma would not produce the dense fibrotic encasement described, and this presentation with a fibrotic mass and no known primary tumor favors fibrosing mediastinitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Lymphoma is an anterior mediastinal 'terrible T' tumor; it does not produce the chronic fibrotic reaction classically linked to Histoplasma.

educationalObjective: Fibrosing (chronic) mediastinitis is characterized by connective tissue proliferation and is commonly caused by Histoplasma capsulatum.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 25-year-old thin man develops sudden chest pain and dyspnea after a marathon without any trauma. A different patient develops mediastinal air after forceful vomiting. The pathologist describes air tracking along bronchial and vascular structures into the mediastinum.
question: Which statement best explains the mechanism and causes of mediastinal air in these patients?

options.text: Mediastinal air always results from esophageal perforation after repetitive vomiting
Ruptured alveoli allow air to track into the mediastinum via peribronchial and perivascular sheaths; causes include spontaneous bleb rupture, trauma, iatrogenic injury, and Boerhaave syndrome
Air enters the mediastinum from the pleural space through a bronchopleural fistula in all cases
Pneumomediastinum is always iatrogenic following central venous catheter placement
Air accumulates from gas-producing bacterial infection of mediastinal lymph nodes

explanation_correct: Pneumomediastinum is the presence of gas, usually air, in the mediastinum. It may be spontaneous from rupture of a pulmonary bleb or secondary to trauma, iatrogenic causes, or Boerhaave syndrome. Ruptured alveoli allow air to track into the mediastinum via peribronchial and perivascular sheaths.

explanation_incorrect.A: Esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome) is one secondary cause, but pneumomediastinum can also be spontaneous from a ruptured bleb, so 'always' is incorrect.
explanation_incorrect.C: Air tracks from ruptured alveoli along peribronchial and perivascular sheaths, not from the pleural space through a bronchopleural fistula in all cases.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pneumomediastinum is not always iatrogenic; it may be spontaneous after a ruptured pulmonary bleb or secondary to trauma or Boerhaave syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Gas-producing infection is not the mechanism; mediastinal air follows alveolar rupture and dissection along peribronchial and perivascular sheaths.

educationalObjective: Pneumomediastinum results from alveolar rupture with air tracking along peribronchial and perivascular sheaths; it can be spontaneous or secondary to trauma, iatrogenic injury, or Boerhaave syndrome.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 30-year-old man has chest pain, dyspnea, and a change in his voice after trauma. On cardiac auscultation a crunching sound is heard synchronously with each heartbeat, and palpation of the neck reveals crepitus beneath the skin.
question: Which finding is most characteristic of this condition?

options.text: Fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, and sternal wound drainage
A pleural friction rub heard over the lung bases during inspiration
Dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds at the lung base
Hamman sign with crepitus on cardiac auscultation and subcutaneous emphysema
An exudative pleural effusion by Light criteria

explanation_correct: Pneumomediastinum presents with chest pain, dyspnea, voice change, and subcutaneous emphysema. Hamman sign is crepitus heard on cardiac auscultation, corresponding to the crunching sound synchronous with the heartbeat described here.

explanation_incorrect.A: Fever, leukocytosis, and sternal wound drainage are features of mediastinitis, not uncomplicated pneumomediastinum.
explanation_incorrect.B: A pleural friction rub is heard with pleurisy or pulmonary infarction, not the precordial crunching crepitus of pneumomediastinum.
explanation_incorrect.C: Dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds suggest pleural effusion, not mediastinal air.
explanation_incorrect.E: An exudative pleural effusion evaluated with Light criteria is not a feature of pneumomediastinum.

educationalObjective: Pneumomediastinum causes chest pain, dyspnea, voice change, and subcutaneous emphysema; Hamman sign is crepitus on cardiac auscultation.
